headline: An S/MIME certificate is linted against the generation it declares itself to be.
summary: The linter read the TLS profile and had nothing for S/MIME, so a certificate issued for email was held only to RFC 5280. The CA/Browser Forum S/MIME Baseline Requirements profile now ships as `cabf-smime`, covering section 7.1.2.3 (a) through (n). Its requirements vary by generation, and a subscriber certificate names its own through a reserved policy identifier, so the rules read that declaration rather than taking a generation from the caller: a distribution point URI or an extended key purpose that conforms under one generation is reported under another.

Added: `pki.lint.certificate(der, { profile: "cabf-smime" })` runs the S/MIME BR v1.0.15 subscriber profile of section 7.1.2.3. The rows reach a certificate unprompted too, because one that asserts a reserved policy identifier has declared itself to be one; a certificate asserting none is left alone. A certificate issued to a subordinate CA carries a reserved identifier as well under section 7.1.6.3, so it is not read as a subscriber; naming the profile in the call still lints it as one.

certificatePolicies (a): the extension is required, should not be critical, and must include exactly one reserved policy identifier, which is also what leaves the generation unambiguous. An `id-qt-cps` qualifier must be a HTTP or HTTPS URL, where the URI scheme tables elsewhere in the section name HTTP alone. This clause asks for a URL rather than a scheme, so a bare `http://` naming no host is reported. An `id-qt-unotice` qualifier must carry `explicitText` and must not carry a `noticeRef`. A certificate issued under a Legacy generation profile on or after 15 July 2025 is reported, gated to the issuance date it states.

cRLDistributionPoints (b): the extension is required and should not be critical, and the URI scheme rule follows the generation. Strict and Multipurpose require every `uniformResourceIdentifier` to be HTTP; Legacy requires at least one and permits others beside it. HTTP means HTTP: the profile writes "a HTTP or HTTPS URL" where both are meant and "the URI scheme HTTP" here, so an HTTPS distribution point does not satisfy it. Having that scheme means being a URI of it, which RFC 7230 section 2.7.1 writes with an authority and no empty host, so `http:crl.example/a.crl` and `http://:80/a.crl` do not satisfy it either. An extension carrying no `uniformResourceIdentifier` at all is reported. A distribution point without one is not, where another point in the same extension carries a conforming URI.

authorityInformationAccess (c): the extension should be present and must not be critical, and it should carry an `id-ad-caIssuers` accessMethod. `id-ad-ocsp` and `id-ad-caIssuers` get a table each, unlike the distribution points, whose single table covers the whole extension. Strict and Multipurpose require every URI of a method to be HTTP; Legacy requires at least one of that method's own, so an HTTP OCSP URL does not answer for a caIssuers list that carries only an LDAP one. An accessLocation that is not a `uniformResourceIdentifier` carries no scheme, so it is reported rather than passed over. The profile asks for this extension at SHOULD where the TLS profile asks at SHALL, so the two report the same absence at different strengths.
basicConstraints (d) must not assert `cA` and must not carry a `pathLenConstraint`.

keyUsage (e): the extension is required, should be critical, and a bit outside the cell for the certificate's own key algorithm is reported. The cells differ, so `keyEncipherment` is conformant on an RSA key and reported on an elliptic-curve one, whose cell gives `keyAgreement` instead, and an ML-KEM key permits `keyEncipherment` alone. The RSA cell also differs by generation: Multipurpose and Legacy admit `dataEncipherment` where Strict does not. A bit set past the nine RFC 5280 named positions is outside every cell and is reported for every key algorithm. A key algorithm the section gives no cell for is held to none.

keyUsage (e) is read as the usage modes the cell states, not as a flat set of permitted bits. A conforming certificate asserts every bit of one mode and no bit outside that same mode, so bits the cell names can still combine into nothing it allows: `nonRepudiation` alone matches no mode, and on RSA `digitalSignature` with `dataEncipherment` matches none either, because `dataEncipherment` belongs to the key-management modes and those require `keyEncipherment`. On an elliptic curve `encipherOnly` and `decipherOnly` appear only in the modes that require `keyAgreement`, which is how the cell states "only if keyAgreement is set". A bit the cell names nowhere is reported by the row above this one, so one violation draws one finding.

extKeyUsage (f): `id-kp-emailProtection` is required, and `id-kp-serverAuth`, `id-kp-codeSigning`, `id-kp-timeStamping` and `anyExtendedKeyUsage` are forbidden at every generation. Under Strict alone, any other purpose is forbidden too.

authorityKeyIdentifier (g): the extension is required and must not be critical, its `keyIdentifier` field must be present, and `authorityCertIssuer` and `authorityCertSerialNumber` must not be. An extension naming only an issuer and serial satisfies the presence rule and is reported by the field rules.

subjectAltName (h and 7.1.4.2.1): the extension is required, must carry at least one `rfc822Name` or an `otherName` of type id-on-SmtpUTF8Mailbox, and should not be critical unless the subject is an empty sequence, which is the one condition that lifts it. An otherName is read for its type identifier, since every otherName carries the same tag and only the type tells a mailbox from anything else.

The optional extensions and the tables that admit them: smimeCapabilities (i), qcStatements (k) and subjectKeyIdentifier (n) must not be critical, and a subjectKeyIdentifier should be present. subjectDirectoryAttributes (j) is prohibited under Strict and Multipurpose and must not be critical under Legacy. The Adobe timestamp and ArchiveRevInfo extensions (m) are prohibited under Strict and must not be critical elsewhere. The Legal Entity Identifier extensions (l) are keyed on the certificate type rather than the generation: both are prohibited on a Mailbox-validated or Individual-validated certificate, the role identifier is prohibited on an Organization-validated one, and neither may be critical where it is admitted.

A cell that reads "Prohibited" carries no criticality sentence, so a prohibited extension that is also critical draws the prohibition alone. A certificate that declares no generation names no cell, and every table the section keys on the generation reads it against Strict, the narrowest of the three.
Changed: The twelve reserved S/MIME policy identifiers of section 7.1.6.1 resolve through `pki.oid`, named for the certificate type and generation each one declares, so an S/MIME certificate reads back with the profile it asserts rather than a bare dotted string. The Legal Entity Identifier and Adobe extension identifiers the profile reads resolve there too.

The fuzz harness for `pki.lint.certificate` drives every profile a caller can name as well as the default rule set, and `pki.lint.csr` has a harness of its own. Both hold the same contract: hostile bytes return a report carrying a `lint/unparseable` finding, never a throw.
Fixed: `pki.lint.certificate`, `csr`, `crl` and `ocsp` take any BufferSource, as every parser in the toolkit already did. They took a `Buffer` alone, so bytes read over the network as a `Uint8Array`, or handed over as an `ArrayBuffer`, raised `lint/bad-input` from the one surface whose data path is documented never to throw. The bytes are snapshotted at the door, so a caller cannot neuter the backing buffer between the check and the read, and a source whose buffer was already detached returns a `fatal` finding like any other unreadable input rather than aborting a scan. A value that is neither bytes, a PEM string nor a parsed object still raises `lint/bad-input`, which is caller error rather than a verdict on a certificate.

`pki.lint.rules("all")` and `pki.lint.rules("default")` return every row rather than throwing `lint/unknown-profile`. The lint verbs read both names as naming no profile, so a caller who linted under one and then asked which rows had run was refused the answer by the registry that ran them.

Naming a profile no longer reads an extension whose value does not decode as one that is absent. Every row asks for extensions by name and the shared decoder answers null for both cases, so `pki.lint.certificate(der, { profile: "cabf-tls" })` returned a clean report for a certificate whose basicConstraints, keyUsage or subjectAltName was malformed, and so did the RFC 9881, RFC 9909 and RFC 9935 profiles. The RFC 5280 row that reports the encoding runs under every named certificate profile now, as it already did for `pki.lint.csr`. Callers who pass no profile were never affected.
